preamble: The voiceless lateral fricative [ɬ] and the labiodental [f] are acoustically similar (both have weak, diffuse frication), and speakers whose language lacks [ɬ] may perceive it as [f]. Davis & Alfaifi (2019) argue that this happened as a regular sound change in Upper Faifi Arabic, where root-initial reflexes of Classical Arabic ḍād (*dˤ, pronounced [ɮˤ] in neighbouring dialects) passed through a devoiced, depharyngealized [ɬ] and were reinterpreted as [f]. The same perceptual equation shows up in English renderings of Welsh ll, such as Floyd from Lloyd (Welsh llwyd 'grey') and Shakespeare's Fluellen for Llywelyn.

examples.note: Classical Arabic root ḍ-b-ʕ. The intermediate [ɬ] stage is reconstructed by the authors, not directly attested; the change applies only root-initially.

sources: Davis, S., & Alfaifi, A. (2019). A different path to [f]: labiodentalization in Faifi Arabic. Papers in Historical Phonology, 4, 45–61. https://doi.org/10.2218/pihph.4.2019.3072
